2. The Dual Ledger
Part identifier: PR-02
Document class: Foundational epistemic architecture
Purpose: Separate occurrence from evidence while defining auditable interfaces between state transition, observation, provenance, reconstruction, residuals, support, claims, and action.
2.1 Why two ledgers are necessary
Part 01 established that retained consequences may be part of a sufficient state. Part 02 adds a second distinction: the state of reality is not the same object as the state of knowledge about reality. A process can occur without being observed; a record can survive while being distorted; a model can be coherent while underdetermined; and a claim can exceed what the surviving evidence supports.
Reality ledger:   Z_n -> A_n -> M_{n+1} -> Z_{n+1}.
Epistemic ledger: Y -> Pi -> F -> R -> S(P) -> C(P).

Figure 2.1 - Dual-ledger architecture. Observation carries information from reality into the epistemic ledger; later claim-informed action can return as an input to future reality without retroactively changing past occurrence.
2.2 Formal objects and semantic types
2.3 Reality, observation, and interpretation are different objects
Let the latent state at event time t be x_t in Omega. A source-specific observation is generated by an operator
Y_i = O_i(x_t).
A useful expanded numerical representation is
Y_i = h_i(x_t) + b_i + epsilon_i,
where h_i is the observation transformation, b_i is systematic distortion or bias, and epsilon_i is stochastic or unresolved error. In historical settings the observation process can also include perception, interpretation, encoding, preservation, translation, extraction, and digitization. The framework does not assume those transformations are perfectly known; unknown components remain explicit uncertainty rather than being silently erased.
2.4 Compatible-state reconstruction
For evidence item i, let B_i(Y_i,U_i) denote the region of record space allowed by its declared uncertainty U_i. The set of latent states compatible with that item is
F_i = O_i^{-1}( B_i(Y_i,U_i) ).
For m admitted constraints, the joint feasible set is
F = F_1 intersect F_2 intersect ... intersect F_m.

Figure 2.2 - Feasible-set reconstruction. Multiple constraints can narrow the latent state set; if their common intersection is empty, they are jointly contradictory in the declared model.
2.5 Theorem 2.1 - Single-source non-identifiability
Proof.
Non-injectivity means by definition that at least two distinct admissible latent states share the same image under O_i. An analysis receiving only that image cannot determine which preimage occurred without additional information. QED.
Plain English.
If two different realities can leave the same record, the record by itself cannot tell you which reality occurred.
2.6 Theorem 2.2 - Monotone narrowing under added constraints
Proof. Every element of F^(m+1) must satisfy all first m constraints plus one additional constraint, so it necessarily belongs to F^(m). QED.
This theorem concerns modeled compatibility, not truth generation. Adding a duplicate or dependent constraint can fail to add new information, while adding an incorrect constraint can shrink the feasible set around the wrong region. Provenance and quality therefore remain part of admissibility.
2.7 Provenance is part of evidence state
An evidence item cannot be interpreted solely by its content. For each item i, maintain a provenance record such as
Pi_i = (u_i, a_i, tau_i, lineage_i, parents_i, transforms_i, q_i, hash_i).
Unknown fields remain unknown. A quoted, translated, summarized, mirrored, reformatted, or AI-generated derivative does not become an independent observation merely by changing presentation.
2.8 Epistemic novelty conservation
If B is a deterministic derivative of A and contains no new independent observation, then conditioned on A it contributes no new empirical information about latent reality X:
I(X ; B | A) = 0.
This statement does not make derivatives useless. A transformation can expose structure, reduce computational cost, improve readability, or create a better decision statistic. The rule is narrower: transformation alone cannot manufacture independent empirical provenance.
2.9 Evidence quality, uncertainty, completeness, and repair
The architecture keeps distinct quantities separate rather than hiding them in one arbitrary score. A candidate admissibility coefficient for evidence item i may include independent dimensions such as provenance independence a_i, empirical quality/calibration q_i, observed coverage m_i, and repair/imputation factor h_i. One bounded composite is
eta_i = a_i q_i m_i h_i,     with each factor in [0,1].
Measurement uncertainty should, where possible, enter the observation likelihood or feasible-set width directly rather than being counted twice through unrelated penalties. The product eta_i is an attenuation bookkeeping device; it is not automatically a probability that the source is true.
2.10 Typed residual state
A single scalar residual can hide incompatible failure modes. Persistent Reality therefore carries a typed residual vector, with components activated as relevant to the analysis:
R = [r_fit, r_scale, r_provenance, r_temporal, r_contradiction, r_imputation, r_transport, r_trajectory]^T.
2.11 Vector-valued support
A single support score obscures the fact that evidence can strongly support one kind of statement and weakly support another. For proposition P define
S(P) = [S_E, S_T, S_Q, S_C, S_M, S_U]^T,
where the coordinates correspond to support for existence, timing, quantity/magnitude, causality, mechanism, and universality. Coordinates are normalized support variables only after their construction is specified. Unless empirically calibrated, they must not be read as probabilities.
2.12 Claim requirements
The wording of a claim determines what support it requires. Represent that demand as
C(P) = [C_E, C_T, C_Q, C_C, C_M, C_U]^T.
For example, “an event occurred” primarily loads the existence coordinate; “event A caused event B through mechanism M in all systems of this class” places substantial requirements on existence, timing, causality, mechanism, and universality. The evidence does not become stronger merely because the sentence becomes more ambitious.
2.13 Componentwise claim solvency
ADMIT(P)  iff  C_j(P) <= S_j(P)  for every required dimension j, subject to hard provenance, temporal, type, and policy gates.
This is a partial order rather than a compensating average. Excess support for existence cannot pay a deficit in causality; excellent fit cannot compensate for future-information leakage; and repeated copies cannot compensate for missing independent provenance.

Figure 2.3 - Schematic vector solvency. A claim fails if any required semantic coordinate exceeds its support interior; strong support in other coordinates does not cancel the deficit. Values shown are illustrative, not calibrated evidence.
2.14 Theorem 2.3 - No cross-coordinate compensation
Proof. Componentwise order requires all required inequalities to hold simultaneously. A single violated coordinate makes the conjunction false. QED.
Plain English.
A claim cannot “average its way” into being supported. Evidence for existence does not prove mechanism; timing does not prove causality; and model agreement does not establish universality.
2.15 Scalar solvency as a special case
The original scalar rule
c(P) <= S(P)
remains valid when the proposition is genuinely one-dimensional and both operands have the same semantic type. The vector rule is the generalization required when a claim contains multiple logically distinct burdens. This also resolves the earlier epistemic-ledger specification failure in which a scale ratio lambda* was incorrectly compared with a residual-derived support ceiling: the operands belonged to different semantic types.
2.16 Evidence Transfer Matrix
Evidence relevance is claim-conditioned. Let evidence items be indexed by i and claim dimensions by j. Define a transfer matrix
W_ij = admissible relevance/support transfer from evidence item i to claim dimension j.
A record can strongly support that a motif, document, measurement, or event report exists while contributing almost nothing to an external causal or mechanistic claim. Fixed source-class weights therefore cannot substitute for claim-specific relevance analysis.
2.17 Contradiction and ambiguity
Disagreement is not contradiction, and contradiction does not identify which source is false. Using the compatible-state sets from Section 2.4:
2.18 Time belongs in the epistemic ledger
Historical evidence requires at least event time and knowledge/admissibility time. A richer bitemporal/multitemporal record can store
R_i = (t_event, t_acquired, t_published, t_available, revision, lineage, Y_i, U_i).
For a frozen replay at time t, define the information set
F_t = sigma( Y_i : t_available(i) <= t ).
A forward-only decision or prediction at t must be a function only of F_t. Later records may improve retrospective reconstruction, but they cannot be silently injected into a claim presented as historically prospective.
2.19 The interface between the two ledgers
The two ledgers are distinct, not isolated. Reality produces observations. Evidence can inform a decision or policy, and that decision can become an input to later reality. Let E_n denote the admissible epistemic state and pi a policy:
U_n = pi(E_n),
Z_{n+1} = T(Z_n,U_n).
Thus a belief, model, or claim can have real causal consequences when an agent acts on it. This does not make the belief retroactively true, nor does it rewrite the occurrence ledger for the past.

Figure 2.4 - Controlled ledger coupling. Evidence is produced by past occurrence; evidence-informed action may influence future occurrence. The arrow of influence does not run backward into past reality.
2.20 Negative precedent as retained epistemic consequence
Failed claims are not discarded from the system memory. Let H_n be the currently viable hypothesis set and F_n the hypotheses falsified by a new test. Then
H_{n+1} = H_n \ F_n  subseteq  H_n.
A failed test is therefore a retained consequence in the epistemic ledger: it narrows future admissible explanations and prevents unsupported rules from being silently reintroduced. 3. The Four Spaces
Part identifier: PR-03
Document class: Foundational ontological-epistemic partition
Purpose: Define occurrence, record, model, and possibility as distinct semantic spaces; specify admissible maps between them; and establish the promotion rules required before a statement may move from one space to a stronger claim in another.
3.1 Why the partition is necessary
The dual-ledger architecture of Part 02 separates reality from knowledge. The four-space partition refines that distinction. It prevents a surviving record from being treated as identical to an occurrence, a fitted model from being treated as the latent process itself, or an imagined/reachable possibility from being treated as realized history. These mistakes share one form: an object is promoted across a semantic boundary without sufficient support for the stronger status.
Occurrence != Record != Model != Possibility.

Figure 3.1 - Four-space architecture. The spaces are coupled through typed recording, modeling, decision, and actualization maps, but no map is assumed lossless or invertible.
3.2 Formal domains and maps
Let the framework use four abstract domains:
The principal maps are typed. A recording or observation operator maps occurrence into record; a modeling operator maps admitted records into a representation; a reachability operator maps a current state into a set of possible later states; and actualization selects or realizes one path from a possibility set through interaction with constraints and inputs.
O : Omega_O -> Omega_R
M : Omega_R x A -> Omega_M,   where A denotes modeling assumptions.
P : Omega_O -> 2^(Omega_O),   the reachable-state correspondence.
A : Omega_P x U -> Omega_O,   actualization under inputs/constraints U.
The use of a power-set-valued reachability map is deliberate: future possibility is generally a set, not a single known point.
3.3 Occurrence space
Occurrence space contains whatever the framework treats as realized state transition or event. It is not restricted to directly observable objects. A latent temperature field, an unrecorded mechanical fracture, a private decision, or a historical interaction may all belong to occurrence space even when no complete record survives. The architecture therefore does not define reality by observation availability.
This distinction is crucial for the later present-centered geometry: history may be re-described, but the realized past trajectory is treated as fixed while the evidence state about that trajectory can continue to evolve.
3.4 Record space
Record space contains traces produced by occurrence through sensing, memory, preservation, communication, or encoding. A record is itself an occurrence - for example, a document was written or a measurement was stored - but its content is not automatically identical to the external event it represents. This dual status is handled by typing: the existence of the record may be certain while the truth of its represented proposition remains uncertain.
y_i = O_i(x) + e_i,
where O_i is the relevant observation/recording transformation and e_i summarizes unresolved error or distortion. For historical material the transformation may include perception, transcription, translation, copying, editorial selection, digitization, or later extraction.

Figure 3.2 - Occurrence-to-record-to-model funnel. Observation can be many-to-one; inversion is therefore generally set-valued rather than exact.
3.5 Record existence is not referent existence
Proof.
Construct a counterexample in which two worlds contain the same record r but differ on whether P occurred. Because the premise "r exists and asserts P" is true in both worlds while P is false in one, the entailment from record existence to P is invalid without additional premises. QED.
Plain English.
A story, image, log, memory, simulation, or document is evidence that the item exists. Whether it is also evidence that the depicted external event occurred depends on how the item was produced and preserved.
3.6 Model space
Model space contains deliberate representations of occurrence or record structure. Models can be descriptive, predictive, causal, mechanistic, statistical, geometric, symbolic, or computational. Their validity is always conditional on purpose, assumptions, data, residuals, and falsifiers.
m = M(D, A, theta),
where D is the admitted evidence set, A is the assumption set, and theta denotes fitted or declared parameters. Multiple distinct models may fit the same records, especially when the observation map is non-injective or the dataset is limited.
3.7 Theorem 3.2 - Model non-uniqueness under observational equivalence
Proof. Any decision procedure restricted to the predicted observations on D receives identical outputs from both models. Therefore no distinction can be made without adding a new test, assumption, or observation outside that equivalence class. QED.
This result motivates adversarial tests, holdout validation, cross-domain transport defects, and negative precedent later in the paper.
3.8 Possibility space
Possibility space is the set of states or trajectories not yet realized but admissible under current constraints. It should be distinguished from unconstrained imagination. A physically, logically, institutionally, or computationally reachable possibility requires a declared constraint set; a merely conceivable narrative belongs to a broader conceptual set until a transport or reachability model is specified.
P^+(z_t) = { z : z is reachable from z_t under declared constraints C_t }.
The reachable set can shrink or expand when retained consequences alter the state, when constraints change, or when knowledge-guided action changes inputs. The set is therefore path dependent whenever the augmented state is path dependent.

Figure 3.3 - Realized history versus future possibility. The past is one realized path; the future is represented as a constrained set of alternatives, not an already-written trajectory.
3.9 Possibility is not prediction
A possibility statement answers whether a state or trajectory remains admissible. A prediction assigns relative expectation, probability, score, or forecast to possibilities. These are different semantic types. The statement "x is reachable" does not imply "x is likely"; likewise "x has high model probability" does not imply "x will occur."
3.10 The past can be fixed while the record changes
The four-space partition resolves an apparent paradox. Historical occurrence is treated as fixed after realization, yet historical knowledge can improve or deteriorate. New archives may be discovered; measurements may be recalibrated; a translation may be corrected; a source may be shown dependent; a previously accepted model may fail. These changes occur in record and model space, not by rewriting the original occurrence.
x_past = fixed;   E_t, F_t, M_t may change with knowledge time t.
3.11 Information loss across the recording map
If O is non-injective, then distinct occurrences can generate the same record. The preimage of a record is therefore a compatible-state set rather than a guaranteed unique state:
F(y) = { x in Omega_O : O(x) is compatible with y within declared uncertainty }.
Information destroyed by O cannot be reconstructed merely by applying more sophisticated language to y. It can only be narrowed by additional independent observations, stronger validated assumptions, or constraints that genuinely exclude alternatives.
3.12 Cross-space residuals
Each transition between spaces can carry its own residual. These residuals must not be collapsed unless a justified aggregation rule is declared.
3.13 Claim promotion across spaces
The most dangerous category errors arise when a statement is promoted across spaces without the evidence required by the stronger claim. Persistent Reality therefore treats claim promotion as a sequence of gates rather than a single confidence score.

Figure 3.4 - Claim-promotion ladder. Each promotion requires additional support; record existence, content, external occurrence, causality, and universality are different claims.
A practical promotion chain is:
record exists -> record contains P -> record supports P -> P occurred -> P caused Q -> P is general/universal.
No arrow in this chain is automatic. Each step has its own provenance, uncertainty, causal, mechanism, and scope requirements.
3.14 Narrative, myth, fiction, and simulation
Narrative artifacts belong naturally in record and model space. They can provide strong evidence about language, motifs, beliefs, design history, cultural transmission, or the existence of a conceptual structure. Their evidentiary value for an external referent is a separate question.
3.15 Worked abstract example
Suppose a sensor network records a transient event. Three sensors produce partially overlapping measurements, and a simulation fits all three. The four-space interpretation is:
Occurrence space: some latent event x occurred, but x is not assumed fully observed.
Record space: three measurements y_1, y_2, y_3 exist with stated uncertainty and provenance.
Model space: a simulation M(theta) reproduces the admitted measurements within residual tolerance.
Possibility space: several latent event configurations remain compatible with the records and model.
A solvent conclusion may be: "The records are consistent with model M and constrain the event to feasible set F." An insolvent conclusion would be: "M is therefore the unique physical mechanism" unless competing models, identifiability, and mechanism-specific tests have been addressed.
3.16 Interaction with the Root Cycle and Dual Ledger
The four-space partition is not a separate theory; it is the semantic layer through which Parts 01 and 02 are interpreted. The Root Cycle evolves occurrence space. Observation creates record-space objects. The epistemic ledger governs provenance, reconstruction, residuals, support, and models. Claim-informed action can alter future inputs and therefore future possibility and occurrence without altering past occurrence.
Occurrence --O--> Record --inference--> Model --decision--> Possibility --actualization--> Occurrence.
This closes a loop while preserving the type of every intermediate object.

4. Current Reality at the Present-Centered Origin

4.1 Why a present-centered frame is useful
Many historical, control, and inference problems are easier to compare when the current state is treated as a common reference. 4.2 Formal definition of the moving origin
Let X : I -> R^d denote a state trajectory in the coordinates selected for analysis, and let tau in I be an audit time. Define the tau-centered representation by
S_tau(t) := X(t) - X(tau).

4.3 Origin theorem and translation invariance
Proof. Substitute t=tau into the definition: S_tau(tau)=X(tau)-X(tau)=0. No dynamical, statistical, or physical assumption is required.

4.4 The origin is not amnesia
Part 01 established that a sufficient state may require retained consequence M(t). Present-centering does not delete that variable. If the dynamically sufficient augmented state is
Z(t) = ( X(t), M(t) ),

Figure 4.2 - Origin is not amnesia. Only the selected coordinate representation is translated; retained consequence remains part of the augmented state.

4.5 What is fixed about the past
The four-space partition of Part 03 makes the temporal claim precise. At audit time tau, realized occurrence prior to tau is treated as already actualized within the model. However, records of those occurrences may be incomplete, revised, newly discovered, re-dated, or reinterpreted. Models of the past may therefore change even when the underlying occurrence is not assumed to change.

4.6 The present as a knowledge boundary
For prospective analysis, the audit time tau also creates an information boundary. Let F_tau denote the information filtration containing only records admissibly available by tau. A present-time estimator must be measurable with respect to F_tau; it may not silently use observations that become available later.
Estimator at tau = f(F_tau),     not     f(F_future).

5. Historical Tangent Geometry
Part identifier: PR-05
Document class: Derived mathematical and estimation geometry
Purpose: Estimate the direction with which a trajectory arrived at each historical audit point, prove identifiability of the anchored quadratic estimator, quantify local fit and curvature, measure realized deflection, and define a solvency boundary for tangent-based projection.
5.1 Problem statement: direction at a historical instant
Part 04 established a family of present-centered frames S_tau(t)=X(t)-X(tau). For a chosen historical audit time tau, shift the local clock so that tau is written as t=0. The estimation problem is then: using only observations with t_i<0 that were admissibly available by the audit time, infer the local direction with which the system arrived at the origin.
v^-(0) := lim_{h -> 0+} [ S(0) - S(-h) ] / h,     when the one-sided derivative exists.
In sampled or noisy historical data the derivative is not observed directly. A local model is therefore required. The canonical baseline in this paper is an anchored quadratic because it is the lowest-order polynomial that simultaneously estimates incoming velocity and local curvature while enforcing S(0)=0 exactly.
5.2 Anchored quadratic local model
S_d(t_i) = v_d t_i + a_d t_i^2 + e_{i,d},     t_i < 0.
For each state coordinate d, v_d estimates the incoming first derivative at the audit origin and 2a_d estimates the local second derivative under the quadratic approximation. The intercept is omitted because the translated frame already enforces S_d(0)=0.

Figure 5.1 - One-sided anchored quadratic fit. Only historical samples are used. The fitted polynomial passes through the audit origin by construction; its derivative there is the incoming tangent estimate.
5.3 Closed-form least-squares solution
For scalar observations y_i with nonnegative weights w_i, define the weighted moments
S2 = sum_i w_i t_i^2,    S3 = sum_i w_i t_i^3,    S4 = sum_i w_i t_i^4,
T1 = sum_i w_i t_i y_i,    T2 = sum_i w_i t_i^2 y_i.
Minimizing the weighted squared error J(v,a)=sum_i w_i[y_i-vt_i-at_i^2]^2 gives the normal equations
[ S2  S3 ; S3  S4 ] [ v ; a ] = [ T1 ; T2 ].
Let
Delta = S2 S4 - S3^2.
Whenever Delta>0, the unique solution is
v_hat = (T1 S4 - T2 S3) / Delta,
a_hat = (S2 T2 - S3 T1) / Delta.
5.4 Uniqueness theorem
Proof. Define u_i=sqrt(w_i)t_i and q_i=sqrt(w_i)t_i^2. Then S2=||u||^2, S4=||q||^2, and S3=<u,q>. Cauchy-Schwarz gives Delta=||u||^2||q||^2-<u,q>^2 >= 0. Equality holds only if q=c u on every positively weighted sample. For nonzero t_i this requires t_i=c for every such sample. Two distinct nonzero timestamps therefore exclude equality, so Delta>0. The 2x2 normal matrix is positive definite and the minimizer is unique.
5.5 Vector-valued state
For S(t) in R^d, use the same timestamps and design matrix for every coordinate. Let V in R^d and A in R^d contain the coordinate-wise coefficients. Then
S(t_i) = V t_i + A t_i^2 + E_i.
The one-sided incoming tangent estimate is the vector V_hat. Under the local quadratic model, the acceleration estimate at the origin is 2A_hat. Because Part 04 established derivative invariance under translation, these derivative estimates are independent of the absolute coordinate offset used before anchoring.
5.6 Fit residual and estimation adequacy
A tangent estimate should never be accepted solely because the normal equations have a solution. Define fitted residuals
e_i = S(t_i) - (V_hat t_i + A_hat t_i^2).
A scale-normalized trajectory-fit residual is
rho_T = sqrt( sum_i w_i ||e_i||_2^2 / ( sum_i w_i ||S(t_i)||_2^2 + eps ) ).
Small rho_T means the anchored quadratic explains the selected local window well in the chosen normalized state coordinates. It does not prove that the process is globally quadratic, that future evolution is quadratic, or that the selected variables form a causally sufficient state.
5.7 Timestamp scaling and conditioning
The columns t and t^2 can become badly conditioned when timestamps are extremely large or clustered. For numerical stability, define a local time scale h0>0 and normalized timestamps u_i=t_i/h0. Fit S(u)=b u+c u^2, then recover
V_hat = b_hat / h0,     A_hat = c_hat / h0^2.
This reparameterization changes numerical conditioning but not the represented polynomial in physical time. The scale h0 must be recorded in the audit manifest.
5.8 Historical tangent field
Repeat the one-sided fit at each historical audit time tau_j. For each j, translate the local coordinates so S_{tau_j}(tau_j)=0 and use only records whose knowledge time is no later than tau_j. The collection
T^- := { (tau_j, X(tau_j), V_j^-, A_j, rho_{T,j}, Pi_j) }_j
is the canonical historical tangent field, augmented with curvature, fit quality, and provenance. The tangent field is not a new history; it is a derived local differential description of the already-realized trajectory under a declared estimator.

Figure 5.2 - Historical tangent field. Each short line represents a local one-sided direction associated with a historical audit point. In a strict replay, each fit uses only data admissibly available before that audit.
5.9 Realized deflection from a historical tangent
Once later history is known, the incoming tangent at tau_j can be tested against what actually followed. For a forward interval h>0, define the tangent prediction
T_j(h) = X(tau_j) + V_j^- h,
and the realized deflection
D_j(h) = X(tau_j+h) - T_j(h).
The scalar deflection magnitude is d_j(h)=||D_j(h)||. This is a retrospective forecast-error geometry: it quantifies how far the realized trajectory bent away from the local incoming direction. It does not explain why the bend occurred.

Figure 5.3 - Historical deflection. The dashed continuation is the incoming tangent ray; the realized trajectory later departs from it. The vertical segment illustrates D_j(h) in one dimension.
5.10 Incoming and outgoing tangent geometry
For a historical audit point with sufficient data on both sides, estimate an incoming tangent V_j^- from pre-audit observations and an outgoing tangent V_j^+ from post-audit observations, using separate one-sided windows. Define the trajectory-change vector
J_j := V_j^+ - V_j^-.
Two complementary summaries separate redirection from speed change:
alpha_j = arccos( <V_j^-,V_j^+> / (||V_j^-|| ||V_j^+||) ),
q_j = ||V_j^+|| / (||V_j^-|| + eps).

5.11 Curvature ratio and local tangent horizon
Under the local quadratic model S(h)=V h+A h^2, the deviation between the quadratic model and its tangent ray is A h^2. Relative to the first-order displacement scale ||V||h, define
kappa(h) := ||A|| h / (||V|| + eps).
For a declared tolerance eta>0, the tangent-only approximation is locally admitted while kappa(h)<=eta. If ||A||>0, an approximate curvature-limited horizon is
h_eta = eta (||V|| + eps) / ||A||.
If ||A||=0 in the fitted model, this particular curvature diagnostic does not impose a finite horizon; other uncertainty, fit, constraint, and support gates still apply. Because norms depend on state scaling, multivariate applications must normalize coordinates or use a declared metric before comparing kappa across dimensions or datasets.

Figure 5.4 - Tangent-solvency horizon. The tangent approximation is admitted only within a declared curvature ratio tolerance. This is a local approximation boundary, not a guarantee of future realization.
5.12 Tangent solvency gate
A prospective tangent projection should close multiple independent gates. Define the tangent-admission predicate
G_T(h) = G_time AND G_prov AND G_ident AND G_fit AND G_curve(h) AND G_constraint AND G_transport.

G_T(h)=1  =>  tangent projection is conditionally admissible at horizon h.
G_T(h)=0  =>  qualify, shorten horizon, or refuse projection; retain the failure reason.
5.13 The live present is asymmetric
At a historical audit point, later data eventually permit V^+ and realized D(h) to be measured. At the live present, they do not yet exist as historical observations. The only historically grounded derivative is V^-(0). A future tangent line is therefore a conditional extrapolation from the past side of the boundary.
5.14 Worked synthetic example
Consider noiseless one-dimensional historical observations generated by S(t)=1.0 t+0.20 t^2 at t=-3,-2,-1, with S(0)=0. The anchored quadratic design has full rank because at least two timestamps are distinct and nonzero. Solving the normal equations recovers
V_hat = 1.0,     A_hat = 0.20,     rho_T = 0.
The instantaneous quadratic-model acceleration is 2A_hat=0.40. With eta=0.10 and eps negligible, the curvature-limited tangent horizon is
h_eta = 0.10 * 1.0 / 0.20 = 0.50 time units.
The zero residual establishes exact recovery of this synthetic quadratic under the stated model. It does not validate the model on unrelated historical data or establish a universal horizon tolerance of 0.10.
5.15 Robust and irregular-data extensions
The anchored geometry is compatible with several disciplined extensions without changing its semantic role:
Heteroskedastic weighting: choose w_i from declared observation uncertainties rather than treating every sample as equally precise.
Robust fitting: replace squared loss with a declared robust loss when outliers are plausible; report that the closed-form least-squares formulas no longer apply exactly.
Irregular sampling: use actual relative timestamps; do not replace them with equally spaced indices unless that approximation is explicitly justified.
Window selection: freeze or cross-validate the historical window rule; changing the window after viewing outcomes can create retrospective overfit.
Higher order: add cubic or spline terms only when data density and validation support the added degrees of freedom; more curvature flexibility does not automatically mean more truth.
State metric: standardize units or use a declared positive-definite metric before computing multivariate norms, angles, or curvature ratios.

6. Observation, Distortion, and Reconstruction
Part identifier: PR-06
Document class: Formal epistemic reconstruction and constraint geometry
Purpose: Define observation operators, uncertainty-aware feasible sets, multi-source intersection, non-identifiability, contradiction, soft reconciliation, provenance-sensitive constraint counting, and claim-level identifiability without forcing unsupported point reconstruction.
6.1 Latent reality and source-specific observation
Let x in Omega denote a latent state of interest. Source s does not generally retain x directly. Instead it produces a record through a source-specific observation process.
y_s = h_s(x) + b_s + epsilon_s.
Here h_s is the source observation map, b_s represents systematic bias or calibration offset when modeled, and epsilon_s represents unresolved error, noise, discretization, or reporting uncertainty. The equation is a modeling template: particular applications must state what each term means and which components are actually estimable.

Figure 6.1 - Latent state to retained record. The observation map and uncertainty model determine a constraint on latent reality; they do not generally furnish an inverse automatically.
6.2 From a record to a feasible set
Let B_s(y_s,epsilon_s) denote the set of record-space values considered compatible with the retained observation and its declared uncertainty. The source-level feasible set is the inverse image
F_s := O_s^{-1}( B_s(y_s, epsilon_s) ) = { x in Omega : O_s(x) in B_s(y_s,epsilon_s) }.
For an exact noise-free observation, B_s may be a singleton. For interval, probabilistic, censoring, or calibration uncertainty it is normally a region. The feasible-set representation preserves ambiguity explicitly.
6.3 Non-identifiability theorem
Proof. Non-injectivity means by definition that two distinct inputs share the same output. Both inputs therefore belong to O_s^{-1}({y_s}). Unless additional constraints exclude one of them, the source-level inverse image contains more than one state. Hence unique reconstruction is not established.
6.4 Multi-source intersection
For m admissible source constraints, define the joint feasible set
F_{1:m} := intersection_{s=1}^m F_s.
Each independently meaningful constraint can preserve, narrow, or eliminate the currently feasible region. The geometry may be highly nonconvex; no convexity assumption is required for the set-theoretic statements below.

Figure 6.2 - Schematic multi-source feasible-set intersection. Each source excludes some latent states while the remaining overlap represents states compatible with all admitted constraints.
6.5 Monotone narrowing
Proof. An intersection contains only elements already in every constituent set. Therefore adding a constituent cannot introduce a state that was previously excluded.
The theorem is purely set-theoretic. It does not say that every added record is independent, high quality, correctly modeled, or informative. A duplicated or redundant constraint may leave the feasible set unchanged.
6.6 Duplicate-constraint invariance and provenance
This elementary identity has an important epistemic consequence: document count and independent evidence count are different quantities. Copies, exports, summaries, translations, or deterministic AI restatements may improve accessibility and error checking, but exact repetition does not create a new latent-state constraint.
If B = f(A) deterministically and no new observation enters, then B is derivative evidence of the lineage A, not a new observational lineage.

Figure 6.3 - Provenance-aware constraint counting. Multiple derivative records from one source lineage should not be promoted into independent observational constraints merely because they appear as separate files.
6.7 Exact contradiction
A collection of hard constraints is jointly consistent exactly when at least one latent state satisfies them all.
Consistent  <=>  F_{1:m} != emptyset.       Contradictory  <=>  F_{1:m} = emptyset.

13.2 Rank-nullity theorem: the unavoidable information loss
This is not a numerical weakness of a particular implementation. It is a structural theorem. If B has full row rank, exactly five independent latent directions can affect the 5-D output and 123 independent directions remain invisible to that output. If rank(B) < 5, the invisible subspace is even larger.
rank(B) = 5  =>  dim ker(B) = 123.
13.3 Observable and nullspace decomposition
For a fixed linear bridge, let B^+ denote the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. Define the row-space projector and nullspace projector
P_obs = B^+ B,     P_null = I_128 - B^+ B.
Every latent state decomposes orthogonally as
z = P_obs z + P_null z.

Figure 13.2 - The kinetic output determines only the bridge-observable component. The nullspace component is erased by the map and cannot be reconstructed from y alone.
A reconstruction from y therefore requires a second model that chooses among the affine family B^+y + ker(B). The chosen prior must be reported separately from the information actually carried by y.
13.4 Fitting a linear bridge without hiding the model
Suppose N paired samples are available, with latent columns X in R^(128 x N) and kinetic columns Y in R^(5 x N). A ridge-regularized bridge solves
B_lambda = argmin_B ||Y - BX||_F^2 + lambda ||B||_F^2.
For lambda > 0, the closed-form primal solution is
B_lambda = Y X^T (X X^T + lambda I_128)^(-1).
This formula is a model-fitting result, not evidence of causal transport. Feature scaling, lambda, sample selection, missing-data treatment, and any low-rank restriction are part of the frozen bridge specification.

A dimensionless symmetric defect is useful for cross-dataset comparison:
rho_B(z,y) = ||y - Bz||_2 / (||y||_2 + ||Bz||_2 + epsilon).

Sigma_y = B Sigma_z B^T.
For a nonlinear bridge y = B_theta(z), the local first-order approximation uses the Jacobian J_B(z):
Sigma_y approx J_B(z) Sigma_z J_B(z)^T.

15.2 Retrospective rolling-origin protocol
For each tested historical origin t, the forecasting loop supplies the model family only with values y_1,...,y_{t-1}. Four deliberately different model views are used where available: persistence, bounded local linear trend, ridge autoregression, and a seasonal mirror. The point forecast is the median of the available model predictions.
m_t = median(m_{t,1}, ..., m_{t,J})
D_t = max_j m_{t,j} - min_j m_{t,j}
The disagreement residual D_t is compared with the 65th percentile of preceding calibration-window disagreement values. The uncertainty interval half-width q_t is the finite-sample 90% quantile of preceding absolute forecast errors. A forecast is committed only if present disagreement does not exceed its historical limit.
COMMIT_t  iff  D_t <= Q_0.65({D_s : s < t in calibration window})
FalseCertainty_t = 1[ |y_t - m_t| > q_t ]

Figure 15.2 - The validation protocol is selective: it may abstain when contemporaneous model spread is unusually high relative to prior disagreement.

16.1 Purpose: from retrospective evidence to prospective discipline
Part 15 established a reproducible retrospective result: a disagreement-based residual gate selectively abstained on harder historical forecasts and improved aggregate uncertainty coverage in the archived campaign. The next scientific question is not whether that computation can be described more strongly; it is whether a rule frozen before seeing new outcomes retains the effect on untouched data. Part 16 therefore defines the protocol that separates discovery from confirmation.
D = D_discovery ⊔ D_validation,   D_discovery ∩ D_validation = ∅
The symbol ⊔ denotes a deliberately disjoint partition. Discovery data may be used freely for model design, threshold selection, diagnostics, and hypothesis generation. Validation data may be used only under a precommitted analysis. If validation outcomes influence the method, those observations cease to be an untouched validation set for that method.

Figure 16.1 - Canonical discovery-to-promotion protocol. Adaptation after the freeze is allowed only by explicitly returning the affected result to discovery status.
16.2 Frozen manifest and experiment identity
A prospective test is identified by a frozen manifest M containing every decision that could materially change the reported outcome. The manifest is serialized canonically and committed by cryptographic hash before the validation outcomes are inspected.
h_M = SHA-256(canonical_json(M))


Figure 16.2 - The frozen manifest is the experiment identity; its hash commits the analysis before holdout outcomes are available.
16.3 Blinding and opaque identifiers
Where labels can reveal entity identity, region, era, source family, or outcome class, the analysis should operate on opaque identifiers. The re-identification map is sealed before the blind run and opened only after the frozen outputs are committed.
b_i = HMAC_k(canonical_id_i)
A keyed digest is preferred to short unhashed aliases because it resists accidental semantic leakage and collision-based aliasing. At least 128 bits of effective identifier strength should be retained when identifiers are used as blinds. The key and mapping are provenance objects, not analysis features.
16.4 Chronology-safe replay and the knowledge-time filtration
Historical replay requires more than sorting by event date. At analysis time t, an observation is admissible only if its knowledge/availability time was no later than t. This prevents later revisions, future publications, and post-event reconstructions from leaking into an ostensibly historical state.
F_t = σ(Y_i : t_available(i) ≤ t)
A_t is admissible only if A_t is F_t-measurable
The bitemporal record from Parts 02, 06, and 15 therefore remains mandatory: event time and availability time are separate fields. Retrospective rolling-origin replay using a final revised dataset is valuable, but it is not equivalent to a true historical information-time reconstruction.
16.5 Falsification battery
A strong result should survive controls that preserve irrelevant structure and fail controls that destroy the structure the claim says it needs. The control suite is claim-conditioned: no single perturbation is a universal falsifier.

Figure 16.3 - Example control-to-claim map. Controls are selected because they target specific assumptions, not because more controls automatically create more evidence.
16.6 Duplicate and narrative injection as epistemic negative controls
The provenance framework makes two unusually direct negative controls possible. First, duplicate injection adds exact or near-exact copies of existing records. Second, narrative injection adds summaries, paraphrases, AI-generated restatements, or symbolic reinterpretations that contain no new observation. A properly lineage-aware system should not award either operation new independent empirical support.
B = f(A), no new observation  ⇒  I(X; B | A) = 0
Support(A ∪ duplicates(A)) = Support(A)   after lineage collapse
Failure of either equality is a provenance bug: the system is manufacturing confidence from repetition or representation change.
16.7 Leakage firewall and adaptation policy

Figure 16.4 - Leakage firewall. Post-freeze adaptation is permitted only by reclassifying the affected analysis as discovery and obtaining a new untouched validation set.
The firewall is procedural rather than rhetorical. Every analysis run records the manifest hash, code hash, data partition hash, analyst-visible metadata class, and whether any holdout outcome was inspected. A changed hash is a new experiment identity. Repeated peeking without a predeclared sequential-testing rule is not a continuation of the same confirmatory test.
16.8 Statistical promotion without independence inflation
The validation protocol must match the dependence structure of the data. Historical forecast errors are serially dependent and may also share macroeconomic or measurement shocks across series. Ordinary iid p-values are therefore not a default promotion criterion. Depending on the design, suitable approaches can include block bootstrap intervals, cluster-aware resampling, predeclared permutation tests that preserve chronology, or hierarchical replication across independent source lineages.
If several candidate metrics or thresholds are tested, the multiplicity rule must be frozen. Family-wise error control, false-discovery-rate control, or a single predeclared primary endpoint are all legitimate choices when their assumptions match the design; selecting the favorable rule after seeing outcomes is not.

PROMOTE(P) = G_freeze ∧ G_blind ∧ G_time ∧ G_provenance ∧ G_control ∧ G_stat ∧ G_claim
If any required G_j = 0, then PROMOTE(P) = 0 and the failure is retained.

17.2 Disagreement, Contradiction, and Conflict
Disagreement is a difference between reports, estimates, models, or constraints. Exact contradiction is stronger: the admissible sets have no common state. A soft conflict is weaker: exact feasibility may remain, but the jointly best reconciliation has large normalized residual.

17.3 Pairwise Consistency Is Not Joint Consistency
Counterexample in R²:
F₁={x≥0},   F₂={y≥0},   F₃={x+y≤−1}
Each pair is feasible: (1,1) satisfies F₁∩F₂, (0,−2) satisfies F₁∩F₃, and (−2,0) satisfies F₂∩F₃. But no point can satisfy x≥0 and y≥0 while also satisfying x+y≤−1. Hence F₁∩F₂∩F₃=∅.

17.4 Minimal Inconsistent Cores
When the full system is inconsistent, the useful object is not the entire corpus but a smallest locally incompatible subset.
C ⊆ {1,…,n} is a MIC iff  ⋂ᵢ∈C Fᵢ=∅  and  ∀j∈C: ⋂ᵢ∈C∖{j} Fᵢ≠∅
A MIC localizes incompatibility. It still does not identify which member is false. Several members may be individually accurate but jointly incompatible because they refer to different times, definitions, populations, units, or latent-state assumptions.
17.5 Provenance-Aware Contradiction
Exact and soft conflict analysis should run on independent provenance lineages, not raw document count. Copies, rephrasings, exports, mirrors, and AI summaries derived from one source are one evidentiary ancestry unless new independent observation enters the lineage.

17.6 Leave-Lineage-Out Conflict Relief
For soft conflict, define the globally minimized objective J*. Remove one lineage ℓ, recompute the optimum, and measure the reduction:
Δ_ℓ = J* − J*_(−ℓ)  ≥ 0
Large Δ_ℓ means that removing lineage ℓ substantially reduces the current incompatibility. It is a localization diagnostic, not a guilt score. A lineage can produce large relief because it is uniquely informative, differently calibrated, temporally misaligned, or genuinely erroneous.

18.2 Typed Transport Maps
Let domain A have state space Ω_A, operations O_A, residuals R_A, unit signatures U_A, chronology T_A, and provenance P_A. Let domain B have corresponding typed objects. A candidate transport is not one number; it is a bundle of maps:
F: Ω_A→Ω_B,   F_O: O_A→O_B,   G_R: R_A→R_B,   G_U: U_A→U_B,   G_T: T_A→T_B,   G_P: P_A→P_B

18.3 Residual-Commutation Defect

τ_F(x,y)=||R_B(Fx,Fy)−G_R(R_A(x,y))||

Figure 18.2 - Residual transport is a commutation problem. The target residual must agree with the transported source residual, not merely look similar.
18.4 Dimensional and Unit Compatibility
Dimensional analysis is a fast refusal gate. Represent the physical dimension of a quantity q by an exponent vector u(q) over a chosen base, for example [M,L,T,I,Θ,N,J]. A lawful unit transport requires an explicit map A_U such that
u_B(F(q)) = A_U u_A(q)
For same-physics unit changes, A_U typically preserves dimension and only numerical scale changes. For abstract dimensionless features, the mapping must explicitly state that the target object is also dimensionless. A numerically convenient equality between incompatible dimensions is not a transport law.
18.5 Provenance and Epistemic Novelty Under Transport
Cross-domain transformation does not manufacture independent evidence. If B=f(A) is deterministically constructed from source evidence A and no new observation enters, then the transformed object remains in the same evidentiary ancestry.
I(X; B | A)=0   for deterministic B=f(A) with no new observation
18.6 Structural Transport Is Not Causal Transport
Preserving a metric, residual, symmetry, or graph pattern does not prove that the same mechanism generates the pattern in both domains. Causal transport requires separately identified intervention or mechanism structure. The canonical claim should therefore distinguish:

rank(B)≤5  ⇒  dim ker(B)≥123

23.9 Dependency-Safe Promotion Theorem
Treat each claim as a node q in a justification DAG with required predecessor set Pred(q). Let Status(q) be bounded by the weakest required predecessor after any declared transport map, unless q receives genuinely new independent proof or evidence. Then a deterministic reformulation, duplicate export, narrative rewrite, or unvalidated cross-domain mapping cannot raise q above the support ceiling of its dependencies.
Status(q) <= meet_{p in Pred(q)} Transfer_p->q(Status(p))
This result is a protocol theorem: it follows from the declared status and promotion rules. It does not assert that the ledger is infallible. Its guarantee is conditional on complete dependency recording, correct type declarations, and honest provenance. Those conditions are therefore part of the canonical audit surface.
23.10 Final Synthesis and Open Boundary
The complete rebuilt framework is not best understood as one equation that replaces existing mathematics or physics. Its contribution is an auditable method for keeping state, history, evidence, residuals, commitments, execution, and interpretation connected without collapsing their semantic types.
Reality has a trajectory. History has a tangent field. Knowledge has a support interior.
Claims have a solvency boundary. Execution has an audit trail. Failure has retained consequence.

Theorem 1.1 - Retained-Consequence Insufficiency.
Let a represented state X_n and admissible input U_n be fixed. Suppose there exist retained states m and m' such that F(X_n,m,U_n) != F(X_n,m',U_n). This Part defines the present-centered coordinate convention used throughout the remainder of the paper. It establishes what the origin means, what it does not mean, how retained consequence survives coordinate translation, and why future possibility must remain distinct from realized history.
Foundational rule.
The present origin is a representation choice, not a physical reset. Translating X(tau) to zero preserves displacements, derivatives, constraints, retained memory, provenance, and all other state variables not explicitly transformed.
Definition 4.1 - Present-centered origin.
For a selected audit time tau, the present-centered origin is the translated coordinate frame S_tau(t)=X(t)-X(tau). By construction, S_tau(tau)=0. The equality is therefore exact and definitional.
Theorem 4.1 - Origin identity.
For every trajectory X(t) for which X(tau) is defined, S_tau(tau)=0.
Theorem 4.2 - Displacement invariance.
For any t1 and t2 in the same translated frame, S_tau(t2)-S_tau(t1)=X(t2)-X(t1). Hence all pairwise displacements are unchanged by the translation.
Corollary 4.2a - Derivative invariance.
If X is differentiable at t, then dS_tau/dt = dX/dt. If X is twice differentiable, the same holds for acceleration. Present-centering changes position coordinates but not local velocity or curvature information.
Theorem 4.3 - Retained-consequence preservation.
A coordinate translation applied only to X leaves M unchanged. Therefore a history-bearing system does not become memoryless merely because its observable coordinate is represented at zero.

Reader status.
This Part formalizes how latent reality is constrained by imperfect records. Exact set-theoretic results are separated from statistical modeling choices. A feasible set may narrow without collapsing to one point, and robust propositions may be identifiable even when the exact state is not.
Core boundary.
Reconstruction is permitted to narrow what remains possible. It is not permitted to manufacture a unique state merely because downstream software prefers a point estimate.
Definition 6.1 - Observation operator.
An observation operator O_s maps a latent state into the record space available to source s. It may discard dimensions, aggregate, quantize, censor, threshold, distort, or otherwise transform the underlying state.
Principle 6.1 - Set before point.
When the evidence supports a region of latent states, the canonical reconstruction object is that region. A point estimator may be added for a declared decision purpose, but it must not replace the underlying feasible set in the evidence ledger.
Theorem 6.1 - Non-injective observation implies possible non-identifiability.
If O_s is not injective on Omega, then there exist distinct latent states x_1 != x_2 with O_s(x_1)=O_s(x_2). Consequently an exact observation y_s=O_s(x_1) cannot, from that source alone, distinguish x_1 from x_2.
Corollary 6.1a - No universal perfect de-distortion.
A universal inverse that exactly recovers every latent state from a non-injective observation cannot exist without additional information, prior restrictions, or side constraints. Apparent recovery may still be possible on a restricted subset, but that restriction is part of the model and must be stated.
Theorem 6.2 - Monotone feasible-set narrowing.
For any additional constraint F_{m+1}, the updated feasible set satisfies F_{1:m+1}=F_{1:m} intersect F_{m+1} subseteq F_{1:m}.
Theorem 6.3 - Duplicate-constraint invariance.
For any feasible set F, F intersect F = F. Repeating an identical constraint cannot further narrow exact feasible-state geometry.
Operational rule.
Collapse exact or near-deterministic derivative records to their provenance lineage before computing independence-sensitive support. Preserve the derivative records for auditability, but do not let repetition inflate evidence interior.
Theorem 6.4 - Contradiction establishes incompatibility, not culprit identity.
If the joint feasible set is empty, the admitted constraints cannot all be true simultaneously under the declared observation and uncertainty models. This fact alone does not determine which source, calibration, timestamp, model, or assumption is wrong.
Consequence.
A contradiction engine must test the joint constraint system, or compute minimal inconsistent subsets, rather than infer consistency from pairwise agreement alone.
Typed interpretation.
Hard feasibility and soft optimization answer different questions. F != emptyset asks whether all hard constraints can hold simultaneously. x*=argmin J asks which compromise minimizes a declared penalty when exact joint satisfaction is unavailable or intentionally relaxed.

Theorem 6.5 - Robust claim identifiability.
A proposition P can be identified as true relative to the admitted constraint system even when the exact latent state is non-unique, provided F subseteq P. Likewise P is robustly refuted when F intersect P is empty.

Theorem 17.1 - Pairwise consistency is insufficient
There exist finite families of constraints for which every pair has nonempty intersection while the full intersection is empty. Therefore pairwise agreement checks cannot certify global consistency.
Theorem 17.2 - Existence in finite inconsistent systems
If a finite family of feasible-set constraints has empty total intersection, then at least one minimal inconsistent core exists. Proof: among all inconsistent subsets choose one of minimum cardinality; deleting any member must restore consistency, otherwise the chosen subset was not minimal.
Provenance rule
Ten contradictory copies of one underlying record are not ten independent contradictions. Likewise, ten agreeing copies do not supply ten independent confirmations.

Theorem 17.3 - Robust claim identifiability
If every feasible latent state satisfies P, the claim is robustly supported despite state non-uniqueness. If no feasible state satisfies P, it is robustly refuted. Otherwise the evidence does not identify the claim and the correct status is unresolved.
Theorem 17.4 - Monotone contraction under hard falsification
If F_n contains only hypotheses rejected by a valid frozen falsifier, then H_(n+1)⊆H_n. The viable search space cannot grow merely by retaining the falsification.

1.1 No automatic promotion
The classes form a governance hierarchy, not a simple numeric ladder. For example, a C2 mathematical
theorem about a simulation may be exact while saying nothing about physical reality. A C5 empirical
result can support a narrow historical claim without establishing a C6 cross-domain mechanism.
Promotion therefore occurs by matching the type and scope of the claim to the type and scope of the
evidence.

1.2 Claim vectors instead of one truth score
The master architecture separates support dimensions because evidence can be strong for one aspect of
a proposition and weak for another. For proposition P define a support vector

S(P) = [ S_E, S_T, S_Q, S_C, S_M, S_U ]^T
corresponding respectively to support for existence, timing, quantity or magnitude, causality,
mechanism, and universality. Let C(P) denote the support requirements of the proposed wording.

ADMIT(P) iff C(P) <= S(P) componentwise
Thus a record may strongly support that an event existed while weakly supporting its precise timing,
cause, mechanism, or universal significance.

1.3 Claim status is versioned
Status may rise, fall, or split as new proofs, measurements, failures, source revisions, or
counterexamples are incorporated. A claim ledger must therefore record the claim text, version, status,
support basis, assumptions, falsifiers, and date of the status decision.

2. Core Distinctions That Must Never Collapse
2.1 Occurrence, record, model, and possibility
Occurrence != Record != Model != Possibility
Occurrence space contains what actually happened. Record space contains surviving traces. Model space
contains organized reconstructions, simulations, or explanations. Possibility space contains alternatives
not yet actualized, including counterfactuals and design hypotheses. A document may be real as an
artifact while fictional in depicted content; a simulation may be exact relative to its code while
empirically false about the world.

2.2 Reality, observation, and interpretation
Reality != Observation != Interpretation
All observations are mediated by access, instruments, perception, preservation, coding, language, or
reconstruction. The framework therefore reconstructs a feasible set of compatible states before forcing a
unique story.

R(Y) = F_Y subset of Omega
A point estimate may be selected only by an explicit rule after the feasible alternatives and uncertainty
have been retained.

2.3 Scale, fit, and support
The Howard projection provides a central example of why quantities must remain semantically typed. If
d = lambda* k + r, then lambda* is a scale ratio, r measures mismatch after scaling, and an alignment
statistic such as cos^2(theta) measures directional correspondence. These quantities cannot be
substituted for one another simply because all are dimensionless.

Rule 2.3.1 - Semantic type safety
Statement. A numerical comparison x <= y is admissible only when x and y belong to the same
ordered semantic type, or when an explicit validated map converts one type into the other.

type(x) = type(y), or there exists validated f: type(x) -> type(y).
Proof / justification. An ordering operation has meaning only after the objects being ordered and
the relation between them have been defined. A floating-point representation alone does not
supply that semantic relation.
Plain English. Two numbers can be dimensionless and still answer entirely different questions.
Status: Foundational governance rule; exact as a formal typing convention.

2.4 The perfect-fit rejection counterexample

1. Process-First Foundation
Part identifier: PR-01
Document class: Foundational mathematics and systems model
Purpose: Define a general state-transition architecture for systems whose future reachability can depend
on retained consequences of prior interactions, while preserving the special case in which ordinary
object-first or memoryless state descriptions are sufficient.

1.1 Scope and claim boundary
Object-first description is indispensable in science and engineering. A point mass can be modeled by
state variables such as position and momentum; a digital controller can be modeled by a finite state; an
inventory can be represented by current quantities. The present framework does not reject those
descriptions. It asks a narrower question: is the chosen state representation sufficient to determine the
transition law relevant to the problem?
If two systems occupy the same represented state but can evolve differently under the same admissible
input because of omitted fatigue, hysteresis, stored internal state, learning, damage, memory, reputation,
prior loading, or another retained consequence, then the represented state is incomplete for that
transition problem. The appropriate repair is state augmentation, not metaphysical reinterpretation.
Canonical claim.
A state description is sufficient only relative to a declared transition problem. Retained consequence
matters exactly when omitted history changes the conditional law of future transitions.

If there exist m and m' such that K(· | X_n,m,U_n) != K(· | X_n,m',U_n), then the conditional transition

2.5 Theorem 2.1 - Single-source non-identifiability
Theorem 2.1 - Non-injective observations do not uniquely identify latent reality.
If O_i is not injective on the admissible latent state space, then there exist distinct x and x' with
O_i(x)=O_i(x'). Therefore the observation alone cannot uniquely distinguish those latent states.
Proof.
Non-injectivity means by definition that at least two distinct admissible latent states share the same
image under O_i. An analysis receiving only that image cannot determine which preimage occurred
without additional information. QED.
Plain English.
If two different realities can leave the same record, the record by itself cannot tell you which reality
occurred.

2.6 Theorem 2.2 - Monotone narrowing under added constraints
Theorem 2.2 - Added admitted constraints cannot enlarge the feasible set.
Let F^(m)=intersection from i=1 to m of F_i. Then F^(m+1)=F^(m) intersect F_(m+1) is a subset of
F^(m).
Proof. Every element of F^(m+1) must satisfy all first m constraints plus one additional constraint, so it
necessarily belongs to F^(m). QED.
This theorem concerns modeled compatibility, not truth generation. Adding a duplicate or dependent
constraint can fail to add new information, while adding an incorrect constraint can shrink the feasible
set around the wrong region. Provenance and quality therefore remain part of admissibility.

2.11 Vector-valued support
A single support score obscures the fact that evidence can strongly support one kind of statement and
weakly support another. For proposition P define

S(P) = [S_E, S_T, S_Q, S_C, S_M, S_U]^T,
where the coordinates correspond to support for existence, timing, quantity/magnitude, causality,
mechanism, and universality. Coordinates are normalized support variables only after their
construction is specified. Unless empirically calibrated, they must not be read as probabilities.

2.12 Claim requirements
The wording of a claim determines what support it requires. Represent that demand as

C(P) = [C_E, C_T, C_Q, C_C, C_M, C_U]^T.
For example, “an event occurred” primarily loads the existence coordinate; “event A caused event B
through mechanism M in all systems of this class” places substantial requirements on existence, timing,
causality, mechanism, and universality. The evidence does not become stronger merely because the
sentence becomes more ambitious.

2.13 Componentwise claim solvency
Definition 2.1 - Epistemic solvency.
A claim P is support-solvent when its requirement vector does not exceed the supported interior in
any required coordinate: C(P) <= S(P) componentwise.

ADMIT(P) iff C_j(P) <= S_j(P) for every required dimension j, subject to hard provenance, temporal, type,
and policy gates.
This is a partial order rather than a compensating average. Excess support for existence cannot pay a
deficit in causality; excellent fit cannot compensate for future-information leakage; and repeated copies
cannot compensate for missing independent provenance.

3.1 Why the partition is necessary

3.5 Record existence is not referent existence
Theorem 3.1 - Record-existence boundary.
From the existence of a record r whose content asserts proposition P, one may infer that the record
exists and that it contains or encodes P. One may not infer P itself without an additional
reliability/observation premise connecting the record to the occurrence space.
Proof.

occurred. Because the premise "r exists and asserts P" is true in both worlds while P is false in one, the
entailment from record existence to P is invalid without additional premises. QED.

A story, image, log, memory, simulation, or document is evidence that the item exists. Whether it is also
evidence that the depicted external event occurred depends on how the item was produced and
preserved.

5.3 Closed-form least-squares solution
For scalar observations y_i with nonnegative weights w_i, define the weighted moments

S2 = sum_i w_i t_i^2,

S3 = sum_i w_i t_i^3,

T1 = sum_i w_i t_i y_i,

S4 = sum_i w_i t_i^4,

T2 = sum_i w_i t_i^2 y_i.

Minimizing the weighted squared error J(v,a)=sum_i w_i[y_i-vt_i-at_i^2]^2 gives the normal equations

[ S2 S3 ; S3 S4 ] [ v ; a ] = [ T1 ; T2 ].
Let

Delta = S2 S4 - S3^2.
Whenever Delta>0, the unique solution is

v_hat = (T1 S4 - T2 S3) / Delta,
a_hat = (S2 T2 - S3 T1) / Delta.

weighted design matrix is preferable when timestamps are poorly scaled or nearly degenerate.

A subset I of admitted constraints is a minimal inconsistent core when its intersection is empty but

6.10 Soft reconciliation when hard intersection fails
Some applications require a provisional compromise even when the hard feasible intersection is empty.
Let delta_i(x)>=0 measure violation distance from constraint i, s_i>0 be its scale, and w_i>=0 a declared
reliability or decision weight. Define

J(x) = sum_i w_i [ delta_i(x) / s_i ]^2,

J* = min_x J(x).

A minimizer x* is the least-penalized compromise under the declared loss and weights. It is not an exact
reconstruction and must not be relabeled as the uniquely true state. J* is a conflict residual conditioned
on the chosen geometry and weighting.
Typed interpretation.
Hard feasibility and soft optimization answer different questions. F != emptyset asks whether all hard
constraints can hold simultaneously. x*=argmin J asks which compromise minimizes a declared
penalty when exact joint satisfaction is unavailable or intentionally relaxed.

sensitivity diagnostic, not proof that the lineage is false. A lineage can be accurate yet genuinely

7.1 The counting problem
A corpus can contain thousands of files while still encoding only a small number of independent
observations. Copies, reformats, summaries, mirrored representations, model outputs, and AI-generated
syntheses may be useful records, but their count cannot be treated as the count of independent
evidence.

"How many records agree?" but "How many independent observation lineages support the claim, under
what uncertainty, and with what claim-specific relevance?"

7.3 Lineage equivalence and duplicate collapse
For an artifact v, let A(v) denote its set of upstream observation ancestors. Two records are lineageequivalent for a given evidentiary purpose when their informative content descends from the same

THEOREM 7.1 | Exact duplicate invariance theorem
If B = f(A) is a deterministic representation change and B adds no new independent observation or calibration
information, then conditioning on both A and B cannot add information about latent state X beyond conditioning
on A alone.

I(X ; B | A) = 0
This does not mean B is useless. A deterministic derivative can improve accessibility, compression,
indexing, numerical conditioning, visualization, or interoperability. The theorem says only that these
benefits are not new independent empirical evidence about X.

7.4 Constraint duplicate invariance
If two lineage-equivalent records induce exactly the same feasible constraint F_A on the latent state,
adding the duplicate constraint changes nothing:

F_A intersect F_A = F_A.
Consequently, exact copies must not narrow a feasible reconstruction merely because they appear
multiple times.

7.5 Structural independence
Structural independence is stricter than file distinctness. Let A_obs(v) be the relevant upstream
observation set. A sufficient structural condition for two evidence items to be independent at the
provenance layer is disjoint relevant observation ancestry:

A_obs(v_i) intersect A_obs(v_j) = emptyset.
This condition is sufficient, not universally necessary. Two records can share an institution, calibration
source, or environmental disturbance without sharing the same observation event; conversely, two
apparently unrelated publications can secretly inherit the same primary report. Statistical independence
and provenance independence must therefore remain separately typed.

7.7 Lineage-collapsed support
Support aggregation is claim-conditioned. A safe default is to collapse exact or near-exact descendants
within a lineage before combining across genuinely distinct lineages. If s_i(P) is a calibrated support
contribution for claim P, one conservative lineage representative is:

s_L(P) = max_{i in lineage L} s_i(P).

across independent lineages depends on the calibrated evidence model; no universal noisy-OR, sum,
product, or Bayesian rule is assumed without its corresponding assumptions.

7.11 The Forge RTL closure signal is an internal invariant, not
independent evidence
The generated RTL updates a primary accumulator by p_g and a complementary accumulator by c_g,
where each selected branch satisfies p_g + c_g = DEN. The commit residual is their sum modulo DEN.

r_n = (w_primary,n + w_complement,n) mod DEN.
THEOREM 7.2 | Closure-by-construction theorem
If r_0 = 0 and every enabled update satisfies p_g + c_g = 0 (mod DEN), then r_n = 0 for every subsequent enabled
step.

r_{n+1} = (r_n + p_g + c_g) mod DEN = r_n = 0.
Therefore solvency_valid is a valid internal integrity assertion for the modular ruler, but it is not an
independent experiment confirming an external physical law. This distinction is precisely what
provenance-aware evidence accounting is designed to preserve.

m_obs,i = 1 if coordinate i was directly observed; m_obs,i = 0 if it was missing, invalid, or imputed.

12.2 Validity semantics: zero is a valid latent value
The audited SnowPulse validation path used std::isnormal on latent coordinates. That predicate rejects
zero and subnormal values in addition to NaN and infinity. Unless the model intentionally forbids exact
zero, this creates a semantic bug: the all-zero state is marked invalid even though zero is a finite value
inside the nominal latent interval.

Recommended predicate: valid(z_i) := isfinite(z_i) AND (-1 <= z_i <= 1).
If subnormals are intentionally flushed for hardware reasons, that should be an explicit quantization
policy rather than an accidental consequence of the validity predicate.

Let P denote the declared projection into the admissible latent ball. A common radial form is

12.10 Shared-memory ring semantics and producer ownership
A ring-buffer push path that obtains the head with load(), writes a slot, and later advances the head with
store() can be correct for a deliberately single-producer design. It is not a general multi-producer
reservation algorithm: two producers can read the same head and target the same slot before either
store becomes visible.

12.11 Deterministic commit pipeline
The canonical execution order is intentionally stricter than the original hot path:
1. Ingest raw coordinates and event metadata.
2. Validate values with an explicit finite/range policy.
3. Freeze m_obs before any repair.
4. Estimate scale/residual only on declared support.
5. Repair missing coordinates and record imputation penalties.
6. Project into the admissible state region.
7. Recompute all transmitted-state metadata on z_tx.
8. Apply typed residual, chronology, provenance, and claim gates.
9. Authenticate the explicit wire record.
10. Commit in deterministic sequence order; otherwise refuse and retain the failure record.

Transport Principle I - Provenance-preserving repair

13.2 Rank-nullity theorem: the unavoidable information loss
EXACT

Theorem 13.1 - Linear bridge nullspace bound
For every linear map B: R^128 -> R^5, rank(B) <= 5 and therefore dim ker(B) = 128 rank(B) >= 123.
Proof. By rank-nullity, dim ker(B) + rank(B) = 128. Because the codomain has
dimension 5, rank(B) cannot exceed 5. Hence dim ker(B) is at least 123.

This is not a numerical weakness of a particular implementation. It is a structural theorem. If B has full
row rank, exactly five independent latent directions can affect the 5-D output and 123 independent
directions remain invisible to that output. If rank(B) < 5, the invisible subspace is even larger.

rank(B) = 5 => dim ker(B) = 123.
PLAIN LANGUAGE
A 5-number kinetic state cannot uniquely encode 128 arbitrary independent latent degrees of
freedom. Any claim that it does must add structure - sparsity, a low-dimensional manifold, temporal
dynamics, priors, or other independently justified constraints.

13.7 Uncertainty propagation and the cost of imputation
If z has covariance Sigma_z and B is linear and frozen, first-order uncertainty propagation is exact:

Sigma_y = B Sigma_z B^T.
For a nonlinear bridge y = B_theta(z), the local first-order approximation uses the Jacobian J_B(z):

Sigma_y approx J_B(z) Sigma_z J_B(z)^T.
Coordinates repaired by imputation must not inherit the same certainty as direct observations unless a
calibrated imputation model justifies it. The observation mask from Part 12 therefore remains part of
the bridge input or uncertainty model rather than being discarded after repair.
EVIDENCE RULE
A complete numerical vector can carry incomplete evidence. Bridge uncertainty must account for
which latent coordinates were observed, which were reconstructed, and how sensitive the kinetic
output is to each class.

Part 05 estimates one-sided kinetic tangents. If B is a constant linear map and z(t) is differentiable, then

y(t) = B z(t) => y_dot(t) = B z_dot(t).

Theorem 13.3 - Constant-bridge tangent covariance
For a fixed linear bridge, differentiation commutes with transport: d(Bz)/dt = B dz/dt.
Proof. B is constant in time and linear, so differentiation distributes through the finite
linear combination defining each output coordinate.

This identity fails in its simple form if the bridge itself changes with time. For B(t),

y_dot(t) = B(t) z_dot(t) + B_dot(t) z(t).
The extra drift term B_dot(t)z(t) is a direct confounder. A periodically retrained bridge can therefore
manufacture apparent kinetic acceleration unless model-version changes are represented explicitly.

tau_v(t) = || v_5(t) - B v_128(t) ||_2
is the natural tangent-transport defect when both tangent estimates are independently available.

For each tested historical origin t, the forecasting loop supplies the model family only with values

preceding absolute forecast errors. A forecast is committed only if present disagreement does not exceed

16.1 Purpose: from retrospective evidence to prospective discipline
Part 15 established a reproducible retrospective result: a disagreement-based residual gate selectively
abstained on harder historical forecasts and improved aggregate uncertainty coverage in the archived
campaign. The next scientific question is not whether that computation can be described more strongly;

design, threshold selection, diagnostics, and hypothesis generation. Validation data may be used only

THEOREM 16.1 - HOLDOUT CONTAMINATION BOUNDARY
If any parameter, feature, threshold, exclusion, stopping rule, or reported metric is modified using the

revised procedure. A new untouched set is required for confirmation.

16.6 Duplicate and narrative injection as epistemic negative controls
The provenance framework makes two unusually direct negative controls possible. First, duplicate
injection adds exact or near-exact copies of existing records. Second, narrative injection adds
summaries, paraphrases, AI-generated restatements, or symbolic reinterpretations that contain no new
observation. A properly lineage-aware system should not award either operation new independent
empirical support.

B = f(A), no new observation ⇒ I(X; B | A) = 0
Support(A ∪ duplicates(A)) = Support(A) after lineage collapse
Failure of either equality is a provenance bug: the system is manufacturing confidence from repetition
or representation change.

The firewall is procedural rather than rhetorical. Every analysis run records the manifest hash, code

NO-PEEKING RULE
The holdout may be evaluated once under the frozen primary analysis, or repeatedly only under a
predeclared sequential design with its own error-control rule. Exploratory inspection is allowed, but
it spends the holdout: subsequent claims from that set are discovery claims.

16.8 Statistical promotion without independence inflation
The validation protocol must match the dependence structure of the data. Historical forecast errors are
serially dependent and may also share macroeconomic or measurement shocks across series. Ordinary
iid p-values are therefore not a default promotion criterion. Depending on the design, suitable
approaches can include block bootstrap intervals, cluster-aware resampling, predeclared permutation
tests that preserve chronology, or hierarchical replication across independent source lineages.
If several candidate metrics or thresholds are tested, the multiplicity rule must be frozen. Family-wise
error control, false-discovery-rate control, or a single predeclared primary endpoint are all legitimate
choices when their assumptions match the design; selecting the favorable rule after seeing outcomes is
not.

EVIDENCE RULE
More analyses do not create more independent evidence when they reuse the same outcomes.
Promotion strength should increase primarily through untouched data, independent lineages, and
successful falsification controls.

17.4 Minimal Inconsistent Cores
When the full system is inconsistent, the useful object is not the entire corpus but a smallest locally

individually accurate but jointly incompatible because they refer to different times, definitions,
populations, units, or latent-state assumptions.

Dimensional analysis is a fast refusal gate. Represent the physical dimension of a quantity q by an

Cross-domain reasoning remains one of the most powerful tools in the corpus, but it becomes rigorous

replication.

Transport what survives the map; retain what fails as residual; never transport more certainty
than the target-domain evidence supports.

independent proof or evidence. Then a deterministic reformulation, duplicate export, narrative rewrite, or
